t: What races do you recommend as good preparation for a Winter/Summer Spine event? And what do you look for when deciding which events to do? (elevation, distance, cut offs, etc.)

The Shropshire Way 80k in April is fantastic, lots of food, multiple checkpoints, 24 hours to complete, open to walkers and runners alike, over 8000 feet of elevation, and although you get written instructions and a gpx the nav can be a bit tricky in places so great head game practice.
It'd actually be a great first big ultra to be fair

I’ve heard good things about - 43% of starters are women according to their website and they have a 48 hour cut off
I did this last year and I’m running again this year Edinburgh to Glamis and volunteering as a marshal for Bamburgh to Edinburgh

Ladies only toilets with products we all need, pit stops well stocked almost every 10 miles absolutely lived it apart from the unseasonable weather poured with rain, fog and very windy made lots of friends along the way great run/walk
I did that last year - they were lovely. Mince and tatties at the 100km check point was the food of the gods 😍
The cut off is stout 32 hrs but local to my as I live 30 mins from the finish line

May be a stupid Q but how do you not fall over on trails? I’ve tripped on pretty much every long run in this training block. Luckily avoided any major injuries (sprained finger doesn’t impact running), but my knees are permentantly scabbed! My elbow has joined the party today. Is it just a hazard of the sport or am I doing something daft that I ...
I'm a frequent tripper. I've been working hard on high knees to avoid catching my toes on roots and rocks
It does make your quads tired though, so maybe some extra quad strengthening work would help
I trip more when I’m tired and more with my left foot- I think it’s improved with strength training over the last few months

Once you've fallen, your proprioception is off and my physio said it can be like that for days. There are exercises that can be done to target this. Try looking a bit further ahead and not directly at the bit just in front of you. Your brain can then be making those adjustments before your feet do. I took quite a tumble coming down from Stoodley...
I trip a lot and a podiatrist asked if I’d broken my leg ever which I had when I was young. She said one leg was longer than the other!! My husband said it was a lazy leg but it is about a cm longer!

Looking ahead rather than directly in front of you is really important to allow your brain to plan, as Marsha has said. It takes a lot of mental focus too - tend to be when we lose concentration that we let a foot drag or misplace a step. Keeping your steps small so your body remains over your feet - this allows you to adjust and recover if you ...

Also, carry germolene and anthisan type products for instant pain relief so you can go straight back to concentrating on where you're going. Personally I find looking at my feet works better than looking ahead - unless I focus on where the person in front of me is placing their feet and watching where they have tripped.

There's also a really big confidence element in descending - doing things like repeat downhill reps over the same bit of ground - starting with something not too technical and progressing in gradient/ length/ technicality can be great at building confidence, footwork and reaction time

Do more technical uphills and downhills - can start hiking, then slow running then go faster on descents. Will get you used to moving on that type of terrain. Practice makes a lot of difference. Good luck, you can do it 💪
If you don't have access to technical terrain, hopping from rock to rock on a beach is a good alternative. There are also drills you can do to work on your agility.
